facts.statement: Sound is produced by vibrating objects and travels as longitudinal mechanical waves requiring a material medium.
Sound cannot propagate in a vacuum because mechanical waves require elastic particles to transmit compressions and rarefactions.
Loudness of sound is proportional to the square of the amplitude of vibration: $\text{Loudness} \propto (\text{Amplitude})^2$.
Pitch or shrillness of sound is determined by its frequency: higher frequency produces higher pitch.
The audible range of frequencies for average human ears is approximately $20\text{ Hz}$ to $20,000\text{ Hz}$ ($20\text{ kHz}$).

definitions.definition: The number of oscillations or vibrations per second, measured in Hertz (Hz).
The maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its central rest position.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Sound travels faster in air than in solids.
common_misconceptions.truth: Sound travels fastest in solids (iron ~5000 m/s), slower in liquids (~1500 m/s), and slowest in gases (~343 m/s).
common_misconceptions.why: Intermolecular particles in solids are packed tightly with stronger elastic bonds.

board_questions.question: If the amplitude of a vibration is doubled, how does its loudness change?
board_questions.answer: Since loudness is proportional to the square of amplitude, doubling amplitude increases loudness by $2^2 = 4$ times.
board_questions.marking_scheme: 1 mark for proportionality formula, 1 mark for 4 times factor

mcqs.question: What is the normal audible frequency range for the human ear?
mcqs.explanation: Human hearing spans the sonic spectrum between 20 Hz (infrasonic threshold) and 20 kHz (ultrasonic threshold).
